newsitem.title: MALTA: Egypt cries foul on EU association agreement.
newsitem.headline: Egypt cries foul on EU association agreement.

text.p: Egypt cried foul on Tuesday on talks with the European Union on an association agreement and said it suspected Europe did not have the political will to offer a fair deal on farm produce.

It would not be worth Egypt's while to sign an agreement which did not provide for fair market access for both manufactured goods and agricultural products, Foreign Minister Amr Moussa told EU and Mediterranean foreign ministers.

"Recent developments in negotiations have caused us grave frustration and stirred our suspicion about a genuine and equitable political will on the European side to conclude an agreement with Egypt that conforms with the true spirit of partnership," he told the conference on Malta.
"I call on the European side to reconsider its position in the negotiations with Egypt in observance of the rules of fairness and genuine interest," he added.

Moussa's robust remarks were in strong contrast to more optimistic assessments by Egypt's chief negotiator, who said last month that Egypt hoped to reach an agreement on principles in time for an announcement at the Malta conference.

The association agreement offered by the European Union would eventually give European manufacturers free access to the Egyptian market but maintain quotas on exports of Egyptian food -- the area where Cairo believes it has the best prospects.

The only obvious benefit to Egypt would be EU aid to help Egyptian industry adapt to the competition and the long-term prospect that its industry could then compete more effectively in other foreign markets.
The most controversial commodities are rice, potatoes, citrus fruit and cut flowers. The EU has increased the quotas but Moussa made it clear they were still inadequate.

"If the agreement does not ensure fair and balanced access for both agricultural and industrial commodities, and make available proper financial support, this will...not justify the burdens Egypt will shoulder," Moussa said.

"We suspect that Barcelona (the Euro-Mediterranean dialogue) is no more than a tactical move...unless the intention is to make the countries of the south pay the price in the long term in return for the assistance they need in the short term," the minister added.

Moussa repeated the Egyptian argument that it was illogical for the EU to restrict imports of Egyptian farm produce when Egypt itself is one of the world's biggest consumers of European grain, meat and dairy produce.
The EU has signed similar association agreements with Israel, Morocco and Tunisia.
